card.hook: Most people march straight into Harborland and start shooting shopfronts. Do the opposite: start 450 m back, where the whole tidy, modern district fits in one shot with plenty of lines to play with.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 450 m north-east of the subject (Harborland). Face south-west and the district opens up ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a straightforward view of the district. Then try 0.5x for more sky and surroundings, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out Kobe Port Tower without walking closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom line so the tall buildings stand up straight.
card.best_time: Morning or early evening usually gives softer, more even light than midday. After dark, give night mode a go if the lights are on, and hold the phone steady for a moment.
card.selfie_here: Head to the waterfront promenade near Mosaic and turn back toward the shopping complex and its Ferris wheel. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the Ferris wheel over your shoulder. For a night-time option, Gaslight Street has old-fashioned lamps that make a popular backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Mosaic waterfront deck, where you can see the Ferris wheel and the harbor, ideally after dark.
card.rules_and_safety: Harborland is generally easy to walk around, but individual attractions may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole scene, then zoom in and find Kobe Port Tower without moving your feet.
card.good_to_know: Harborland is a shopping district in Chuo-ku, Kobe, and Kobe Port Tower stands here. The land was once a freight yard belonging to the Japanese National Railways. The yard was removed in 1982 and the shopping district opened in 1992.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 450 m north-east of the subject (Harborland). Face south-west and the district opens up ahead of you.

card.hook: Dumplings, buns and pastries are piled up on display, and a gate rises over the street ahead of you. In Kobe's Chinatown there's something worth a photo every few steps, so your phone will fill up fast.
card.stand_here: Stand near 南京東路, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Turn slowly and look down each street before you pick your shot.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for the gates and the packed streets, and 1x for everyday scenes. Go to 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the zodiac carvings, the lions and the food on display.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the food or carving, then slide it a little darker if the bright shopfronts wash out your picture.
card.best_time: Try earlier in the day for emptier streets and easier wide shots. Late afternoon into evening is good for atmospheric shots with the shops lit up, and night mode can help if it's dim.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie in Nankinmachi Square with the Azumaya pavilion behind you. Or head to Chang'an Gate on the east side, opposite the Daimaru department store, and put the gate behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the landmark fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the central square facing the octagonal pavilion, while you pose in front of it so you and the pavilion both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The streets are open to walk through, but individual shops, stalls and any events have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the zodiac animal for your birth year among the 12 stone carvings, and get a close-up of it looking its best.
card.good_to_know: Nankin-machi began in 1868, when Kobe's port opened to foreign traders and Chinese settlers made their home at the western edge of the foreign district. The area was destroyed in the Second World War and rebuilt by the Chinese community that stayed on. It was badly hit again by the 1995 Great Hanshin earthquake, then rebuilt once more.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near 南京東路, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Turn slowly and look down each street before you pick your shot.

card.hook: Kobe Port Tower is a slim red tower that looks like it's been cinched at the waist, and it's meant to, because its shape recalls a Japanese hand drum. That red really pops against sky or water, so it's an easy one to love.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon near 浜手バイパス, about 190 m north-east of the subject, and face south-west. The tower will be right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole tower with some surroundings. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of that curvy shape, and use 0.5x only if you walk up close and want the full height in the frame.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the tower up with a vertical line, and tap the tower, then drag the slider to darker if the sky is washing out so the red stays rich.
card.best_time: Late afternoon through dusk is lovely: the light is softer, and you can hang around while the sky darkens and the tower's lights come on. Use night mode after dark and hold your phone steady against something solid.
card.selfie_here: Try the BE KOBE monument in Meriken Park, on the seaside roughly between the tower and the Kobe Maritime Museum. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze in the big letters and the sea, and check whether the tower sneaks in over your shoulder, because we haven't confirmed it does from there.
card.ask_someone: On the lawn in Meriken Park, hand your phone to a passer-by, stand with the tower behind you, and ask them to step back and hold the phone upright so the full tower fits.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography in Meriken Park is free and open to all. If you go up the tower, photos on the outdoor gallery can only be taken through the glass.
card.challenge: Find a spot where the tower's vertical lines sit perfectly straight on a grid line, then take one shot with a bit of foreground so it feels like you were really there.
card.good_to_know: The tower is 108 m tall, was designed by Nikken Sekkei and was completed in 1963. It was the first tower built with a pipe lattice, and its 32 red steel staves are said to symbolise a welcome for vessels returning to shore. It reopened on 26 April 2024 after a long renovation and seismic work.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the phone icon near 浜手バイパス, about 190 m north-east of the subject, and face south-west. The tower will be right in front of you.

card.hook: Most city parks hide the sky behind trees. Meriken Park does the opposite: it hands you a big open stretch of sky and harbour water, and all you have to do is pick one landmark to star in your photo.
card.stand_here: Near 浜手バイパス, stand about 80 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. The middle of the park is then laid out in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the waterfront and buildings in together. Use 1x for most shots, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out details like the top of the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom line, so the sky or water gets room to breathe.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk usually gives softer light, and you can switch on night mode for the lit-up harbour. Any clear day works well, though.
card.selfie_here: Head to the BE KOBE monument on the seaside of the park, roughly between the Port Tower and the Maritime Museum. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and angle yourself so the harbour is behind you. It's the park's best-known photo backdrop, and it gets busy, so early or a weekday is easier.
card.rules_and_safety: The memorial is a place of remembrance, so keep photos respectful and don't pose in front of it. Ask staff before taking photos inside the Kobe Maritime Museum, and check the official site for entry rules at the tower and museum.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole harbour, then walk a few minutes along the waterfront and see if you can make the same landmark look like a different picture.
card.good_to_know: Meriken Park sits on Kobe's harbour front and holds the Kobe Port Tower, the Kobe Maritime Museum and a memorial to the victims of the Great Hanshin earthquake. The name comes from 'American', which was commonly rendered as 'Meriken' in the Meiji era, so it makes a nice photo caption. The Hotel Okura Kobe and the Kobe Meriken Park Oriental Hotel are in the park too.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Near 浜手バイパス, stand about 80 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. The middle of the park is then laid out in front of you.

card.hook: Walk up from the street in central Kobe and a huge vermilion gate stops you in your tracks, with the shrine's trees showing right behind it. It's the picture everyone takes, and it really does look that good.
card.stand_here: Stand at the front of the red tower gate (楼門) on the street side, facing the shrine. Keep the gate dead centre.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the gate head-on. If the gate is too big to fit, tap 0.5x and keep your phone level. For the torii tunnel inside, try zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines so the gate pillars stay straight, tap the red of the gate, then slide it a touch darker so the vermilion stays rich.
card.best_time: Weekdays and earlier in the day are your best bet, because the torii row can get crowded at weekends. If it's busy, wait a moment and shoot between groups.
card.selfie_here: Take it inside the red torii tunnel at the Inari shrine in the northeast corner, where stone foxes sit nearby. Use the front camera and hold it a little low so the red gates glow over your shoulder; one guide says there are fewer people behind you here, though there's a concrete wall along one side. Or try the open grass in front of the main hall, with the buildings behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take it while you stand on Ikuta Road, the street running straight up to the shrine, with the entrance torii in the distance behind you; it's worth checking the spot on the ground.
card.rules_and_safety: No photos inside the main hall, and a sign on the grounds warns about photography, so check it before you shoot. Try not to stand on the central path in front of the shrine; leave it free for worshippers.
card.challenge: Get the gate with both pillars perfectly straight, then hunt down a fox statue by the torii tunnel for bonus points.
card.good_to_know: Ikuta Shrine is a Shinto shrine and may be one of the oldest in Japan. The Nihon Shoki says Empress Jingū founded it at the start of the 3rd century AD to honour the kami Wakahirume. Parts of the Battle of Ichi-no-Tani were fought in and around the grounds, and markers in the Ikuta forest behind the shrine recall it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the front of the red tower gate (楼門) on the street side, facing the shrine. Keep the gate dead centre.

card.hook: Squint a little and this hotel looks like an ocean liner that pulled up beside Meriken Park and decided to stay. That's exactly what its designers were going for.
card.stand_here: Stand about 70 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east towards the Kobe Meriken Park Oriental Hotel. It's about a minute on foot from the Harborland and Meriken Park waterfront.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole building in. If you're close and it won't fit, tap 0.5x, and use 2x for details on the front.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the horizon up with a grid line, then tap the hotel and drag it a little darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk is lovely, when the sky softens and the hotel's lights start to show. Early morning is usually quieter if you want fewer people in the frame.
card.selfie_here: Head to the BE KOBE monument beside the water in Meriken Park. Use the front camera, try 0.5x so the letters fit, and put the hotel rising behind the lettering over your shoulder. People queue for this one, so be patient.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the open ground in front of the hotel's curved front on the Meriken Park side, while you stand a few steps in front of the hotel for a front-on shot.
card.challenge: Get the whole hotel and the Kobe Port Tower in one frame with the horizon dead level. Bonus points if nobody walks through it.
card.good_to_know: The hotel has 14 floors and 331 rooms, and Takenaka Corporation shaped it to look like a luxury liner. It opened in June 1995, only six months after the Great Hanshin earthquake destroyed much of the city, so it has a special place in Kobe's story. It's a working hotel, so it's best photographed from the outside.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 70 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east towards the Kobe Meriken Park Oriental Hotel. It's about a minute on foot from the Harborland and Meriken Park waterfront.

card.hook: Picture a minaret and an onion-shaped dome popping up between old Western-style houses. That's Kobe Mosque, and yes, it's as charming as it sounds.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, in the mosque's eastern parking lot, at the edge and out of the way of cars. The mosque lies just to the south-west of you, so face that way and you'll see the minaret with its balcony on the right, the dome on the left and the facade in the middle.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which fits the minaret, dome and facade together. If the car park is cramped and you can't step back, go to 0.5x and keep the mosque away from the edges so it doesn't look stretched. Try 2x or more for a closer shot of the dome or the minaret's balcony.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the minaret on the right-hand line and the dome on the left, and keep your phone level so the minaret stands up straight.
card.best_time: Pick a moment when the car park is quiet and no prayer service is on. Check for posted service times when you arrive, or ask at the mosque.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and hold your phone a little low, so the building stands up behind you. Try 0.5x if your front camera has it, and keep the mosque over your shoulder rather than squeezed against the edge of the frame.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the edge of the eastern parking lot with the minaret in the upper right and the dome in the upper left of their screen, while you pose in front of the building.
card.rules_and_safety: The east side is the mosque's own car park, so treat it as private: stay at the edge and keep clear of vehicles and doorways. Don't take photos during a prayer service, and don't photograph the inside unless you've been given permission.
card.challenge: Get one frame with the minaret perfectly upright, the dome on the other grid line and not a single car or stranger in sight. Patience is the real skill here.
card.good_to_know: Kobe Mosque is Japan's first mosque, founded in October 1935. It was designed by Czech architect Jan Josef Švagr and built in reinforced concrete. It came through the 1945 air raids and the 1995 Great Hanshin earthquake, so some people call it the "Miracle Mosque".
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, in the mosque's eastern parking lot, at the edge and out of the way of cars. The mosque lies just to the south-west of you, so face that way and you'll see the minaret with its balcony on the right, the dome on the left and the facade in the middle.

card.hook: This old bank still looks like it's guarding something valuable, and from the street it's the columns and stonework that make the photo. Get low, tilt up, and the whole front looks grand.
card.stand_here: Stand at street level on Kyomachisuji, about 100 m north-east of the Kobe City Museum, and face the museum. If you can, cross to the opposite side of the street so the whole frontage fits in one shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole front in from across the street. Then try 1x for a tidier, less stretched look, and zoom 2x or 5x for the stonework and entrance details, if your phone has them.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so nothing leans.
card.best_time: Go after dark, when the building is lit up and looks very different from the daytime version. Daytime still works, so don't skip it if that's when you're passing.
card.selfie_here: Try the forecourt outside the main entrance, next to the bronze Jean de Fiennes sculpture. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the columned facade over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the east-side sidewalk of Kyomachisuji, opposite the museum, while you stand in front of the facade so the whole building fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos from the street are fine. Inside, photography is generally not allowed, especially in special exhibitions, and opening days vary between sources, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Hold your phone low, tilt it up, and take a photo where every column stands perfectly straight. Then turn north and grab the Hankyu Kobe-Sannomiya Building as your bonus shot.
card.good_to_know: The building dates from 1935 and was put up as the Kobe branch of the Yokohama Specie Bank. It became a museum in 1982. Inside are nearly thirty-nine thousand items, including old maps, Nanban art, and Yayoi-period dōtaku from Sakuragaoka that are a National Treasure.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at street level on Kyomachisuji, about 100 m north-east of the Kobe City Museum, and face the museum. If you can, cross to the opposite side of the street so the whole frontage fits in one shot.

selfie_spots.why: The museum's Doric-columned granite front is the main photogenic feature, and the sculpture sits just outside the entrance, so it can serve as a visible frame for a close-up with the building behind. No page explicitly recommends this as a selfie spot.

card.hook: Imagine a mile of shopfronts, glowing signs and busy shoppers, all under one roof and all pointing the same way. That's Motomachi, and it's made for photos with depth.
card.stand_here: Stand about 370 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map near 元町商店街 (Motomachi Shopping Street), and face west. Pick a spot near the middle of the street, a little to one side, so you're out of everyone's way, then point your phone down the arcade.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the whole length of the covered street. Switch to 1x for everyday street scenes, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out signs and details further along.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the roof beams and shopfronts with them so everything stays nice and straight.
card.best_time: Quieter times make it easier to get a clear shot down the street. Evening is great for glowing signs, but expect more people. The roof means you can shoot in almost any weather.
card.selfie_here: Try the east entrance, where the arcade begins beside Daimaru department store on Koikawasuji street. Use the front camera at 0.5x and turn so the arcade stretches out behind your shoulder. Nobody has confirmed the best angle here, so take a few test shots to check the framing.
card.rules_and_safety: The street itself is public, but shops, restaurants and buildings have their own rules, so check with them before photographing inside. Keep moving enough that you don't block people walking through, and it's polite to ask before photographing individuals.
card.challenge: Take one long shot down the arcade, then one close-up of a single sign that grabs you. Bonus points if a passer-by walks into the first shot at just the right moment.
card.good_to_know: Motomachi sits between Mount Rokkō and the port, and many trading companies were based here in the 19th century. It's often compared with Motomachi in Yokohama, Ginza in Tokyo and Shinsaibashi in Osaka. Right next door are Nankinmachi (Kobe Chinatown) and the old foreign settlement of Kyū-kyoryūchi, where some buildings from that era are now restaurants or coffee shops.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 370 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map near 元町商店街 (Motomachi Shopping Street), and face west. Pick a spot near the middle of the street, a little to one side, so you're out of everyone's way, then point your phone down the arcade.

card.hook: Most people see Kobe Luminarie from inside the crowd, shuffling under glowing arches. Go up 24 floors and you see the whole thing laid out like a glittering map, with no elbows in your shot.
card.stand_here: Head to the 24th-floor observation lobby of Kobe City Hall No. 1 Building (神戸市役所1号館). Face the window that looks down over the light route and Higashi Yuenchi Park.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole route and park in one shot. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the arches and the crowd below. Down at street level, zoom 0.5x helps you fit in the full arches.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest lights, then slide to darker so the bulbs keep their colours instead of turning white.
card.best_time: Go after dark, when the lights are on. They're only lit for a few hours each evening, so arrive early. The next edition is listed as roughly late January to early February 2027, so confirm dates and hours on the official site.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the front of the light tunnel, at the start of the arched corridor on Nakamachi-dori, before you walk in. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a bit low so the glowing arches rise up behind your shoulder. The festival layout changes from year to year, so check where the arches are this time.
card.ask_someone: In the open lawn area of Higashi Yuenchi Park, ask your helper to stand on the lawn facing the light corridor, while you stand in front of them with the corridor behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos and video are fine, but don't block foot traffic. Staff may ask you to keep moving, and the corridor is one-way, so you can't double back. The City Hall lobby's opening hours aren't confirmed, and some festival areas may be ticketed, so check the official site.
card.challenge: Take one photo from above where the glowing route runs diagonally across the frame, then find the tiny people at the bottom for scale.
card.good_to_know: Kobe Luminarie began in 1995 as a tribute to the people of Kobe after the Great Hanshin earthquake. The lights were a gift from the Italian Government, and more than 200,000 hand-painted bulbs are lit in arches and walls. The display usually stays up for about two weeks.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the 24th-floor observation lobby of Kobe City Hall No. 1 Building (神戸市役所1号館). Face the window that looks down over the light route and Higashi Yuenchi Park.

card.hook: Want a photo that shouts 'port city' without any effort? Here you can fit the whole museum and a big slice of sky into one frame, and your phone will love it.
card.stand_here: Stand about 50 m south of the museum, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The museum building is your subject.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the whole building and the sky are in view. If you can't fit it all in, drop to 0.5x, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out roof shapes and details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then slide the brightness down a touch if the sky is washed out, so the sky keeps its colour and the building doesn't turn into a dark shape.
card.best_time: Try a few different times of day and check how the light hits the building from this side. Early evening can add warm colour, and after dark you can use night mode and tuck your elbows into your body to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the BE KOBE monument on the seaside of Meriken Park, roughly between Port Tower and the Maritime Museum. Guides call it the park's most popular photo backdrop, and it's lit up at night. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and check what's behind your shoulder before you tap, because we haven't confirmed the museum sits directly behind you here. It can get busy at peak times.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on the sea side of Meriken Park near the Starbucks area, then step back toward the museum so it fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask staff before taking photos inside the museum or at the Kawasaki World exhibits, and check any signs, as some exhibits may have restrictions.
card.challenge: Take one landscape shot and one portrait shot of the building, with perfectly straight sides and no stranger's head in the frame. Gridlines will help, and patience wins.
card.good_to_know: The museum is devoted to the history of Japanese shipping and the story of Kobe harbour itself. The Yamato 1 and the TSL Hayate, two former exhibits, were removed in 2016, so you won't see them any more. It's a quick stop, and it's worth checking the official site for access and entry details before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 50 m south of the museum, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The museum building is your subject.

card.hook: Round one corner and the everyday street suddenly has Western-style houses lined up along it, some still lived in, some open for you to wander through. Don't wait for one perfect view here, because the whole walk is the photo.
card.stand_here: Start near 天神坂 and stand about 380 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. Then stop wherever a house is clear of people and parked vehicles, and shoot from the lane across from it.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for whole houses and street scenes. Switch to zoom 0.5x in narrow lanes where you can't step back, then zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for windows, doorways, balconies and roof lines.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines so the walls and rooflines stay straight, and take a few frames of each house from slightly different distances.
card.best_time: Go early in the day for fewer people in your frames. Soft daylight, like a bright overcast day, is lovely on the walls and details.
card.selfie_here: Head to Kitano-cho Square (北野町広場) at the top of the stairs and stand beside the bronze musician statue with the Weathercock House behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the house over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in Kitano-cho Square to frame the whole Weathercock House, while you pose by the bronze musician statue at the top of the stairs.
card.rules_and_safety: Photo rules differ from house to house, so check the signs, and some places ask for no flash. Photography of everything is allowed at Uroko Museum. Keep to the public lanes and respect the homes that are still private residences.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of a house in its street, then find a single detail on it, like a window, a door or a balcony, and make that your second photo.
card.good_to_know: Ijinkan can describe any foreign house of the late Meiji and early Taishō eras in Japan, but it's most often used for the ones here, because so many have survived. Hakodate and Nagasaki have similar districts, though they're not as well preserved. Many houses are open to visitors, which makes this one of Kobe's main places for tourists.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start near 天神坂 and stand about 380 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. Then stop wherever a house is clear of people and parked vehicles, and shoot from the lane across from it.

card.hook: You don't need a toddler in tow to enjoy a building that's all about Anpanman. The bright, cheerful frontage is a fun photo subject even if you never step inside.
card.stand_here: Stand near ハーバーロード, about 35 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. That gives you the whole frontage from a little way back.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole frontage. The building is wide (roughly 94 metres across), so switch to zoom 0.5x if it won't fit. Then walk closer and use zoom 2x for a detail or two.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the building up with them so the walls don't lean, leaving a little space around the edges.
card.best_time: Daylight is best for bright colours, and earlier in the day is usually calmer. Take a quick look at your shot and retake it if the sky has washed out.
card.selfie_here: Head to the forecourt in front of the building, beside the Anpanman statue that greets visitors before the entrance. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and keep the museum behind you over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a shot of you with the painted wall, ask a passer-by to shoot from the canal side of the museum in Harborland while you stand with the wall behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos and video are allowed for personal use. Flash isn't allowed during the stage performance, and please take care not to disturb other visitors while you photograph. If other people's children are in the scene, keep them small in the frame or turned away from the camera. If you're going inside, check the official site first for entry details.
card.challenge: Take one clear shot of the whole frontage, then find one small detail up close and see if a friend can guess what it is.
card.good_to_know: The museum is built around Takashi Yanase's Anpanman characters, which are hugely popular with children in Japan. It's one of five such complexes, the others being in Yokohama, Sendai, Nagoya and Fukuoka. Kobe's opened in 2013, which makes it the newest of the five.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near ハーバーロード, about 35 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. That gives you the whole frontage from a little way back.

card.hook: Yes, those lampposts really do tilt, and no, your phone isn't broken. They stand on a preserved quay about 60 m long, so slow down and take it in before you start snapping.
card.stand_here: Stand near 神戸港震災メモリアルパーク (Port of Kobe Earthquake Memorial Park), about 40 m south-west of the subject, right at the phone icon on the map. Face north-east.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the "this is the place" shot. Switch to 0.5x if you want more of the open space in the frame, and use 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for details like a plaque or a lamppost.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the horizon level, then tap the brightest part of the screen and slide it a touch darker so pale surfaces and sky keep their detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives you softer light and fewer people. Midday sun can make everything look flat and harsh.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, hold your phone a little lower and switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it on the front, so the memorial fits behind your shoulder. Keep it quick and quiet, and check that nobody else is in your frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed, but treat this as a place of remembrance rather than a casual tourist stop. Wait for a clear moment instead of asking people to move, and don't photograph anyone close up without asking. Check the official site for opening arrangements and any restrictions before you go.
card.challenge: Find a tilted lamppost, put it on a gridline, and keep your horizon dead level so the only lean in the photo is the lamppost's.
card.good_to_know: This memorial sits in the northeast corner of Meriken Park. Look for the round black 05:46 disc monument, the 'Hishō no Suzaku' sculpture and the stone pillars listing victims' names. Don't mix it up with Minato no Mori Park, which is a different place.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near 神戸港震災メモリアルパーク (Port of Kobe Earthquake Memorial Park), about 40 m south-west of the subject, right at the phone icon on the map. Face north-east.

selfie_research.notes: Landmark matched to Port of Kobe Earthquake Memorial Park (2 Hatobacho, Chuo-ku, Kobe), in the northeast corner of Meriken Park. The given coordinates match its listed geo position (34.683683, 135.190065) on LIVE JAPAN. Do not confuse it with Minato no Mori Park, which Navitime also calls 'Kobe Earthquake Memorial Park' (Onohama-cho). No page I found names a specific selfie spot with the memorial behind the visitor, or a specific spot for a passer-by to photograph the visitor with the whole memorial in frame, so both fields are left empty rather than guessed. Pages that name features you could build on: the preserved ~60 m quay with tilted lampposts, the round black 05:46 disc monument, the 'Hishō no Suzaku' sculpture, and stone pillars listing victims' names. The BE KOBE monument is a popular photo spot, but it is in Meriken Park and does not have this memorial behind it. Sources on photography etiquette: one says photography is allowed but the site should be treated respectfully and not as a casual tourist spot, and another says photography is generally allowed but casual or intrusive shooting should be avoided. No page states selfie stick or tripod rules, so none are reported. Sources consulted include hyogo-tourism.jp, atlasobscura.com, wanderlog.com, livejapan.com, and airial.travel.

card.hook: Picture a 1907 stable sitting upside down in a pond, perfectly still, with a whole garden's worth of green wrapped around it. That's the Sōraku-en moment, and it's right in the middle of Kobe.
card.stand_here: Walk to the pond edge, where the phone icon on the map sits right at the subject. Face the old Kodera Stable across the water and let its reflection fill the bottom of your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the stable and its reflection. Switch to 0.5x to fit the pond, trees and buildings into one picture. For the teahouse across the water, try zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the stable on one third of the screen and keep your phone level so the water looks flat.
card.best_time: Soft morning light is lovely for the reflection. In November the garden is popular for its autumn illumination, so expect more people and check the dates before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the little stone bridge in the middle of the pond, with the garden and pond behind you. Or stand at the pond shore with the Kodera Stable in the background. Use the front camera, and 0.5x if you want more of the scene to squeeze in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pond side facing the stable, so the whole building and the pond fit in the frame, while you stand at the water's edge with the stable behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The historic buildings can only be photographed from the outside, so keep to the paths and the water's edge.
card.challenge: Take one photo where nobody can tell at first glance which stable is the real one and which is the reflection.
card.good_to_know: Sōraku-en is a stroll garden, so a path leads you around the central pond. It was once part of the home of Kodera Yasujirō and has belonged to the city since 1941. Most of the old house was lost in the war, but the 1907 stable survived and is now an Important Cultural Property.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the pond edge, where the phone icon on the map sits right at the subject. Face the old Kodera Stable across the water and let its reflection fill the bottom of your screen.

selfie_research.notes: Sources do not give exact standing points for the selfie spots or the photographer spot; the stone bridge and stable locations are from general descriptions, so check them on the ground. No page mentions selfie stick rules. Sources differ on the address (5-3-1 on WikiVisually vs 5-chome-3-1 on other pages) and on the fee (300 yen in most reviews, 300–500 yen on one blog). Fees and hours were not verified against the official site.

card.hook: Picture a row of bronze figures with the harbour behind them and a few strangers wandering through your shot. That's Kobe Kaientai, and it's a nice place to slow down for a minute.
card.stand_here: Stand about 45 m north-east of Kobe Kaientai, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Then walk towards it for a closer shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view. If the space is tight, switch to 0.5x. If something is in the way, try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the subject from further back.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and put the subject on one of the lines instead of dead centre.
card.best_time: Daylight is the simplest way to get a clear, sharp shot. In the evening, use night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the seaward side of the Kobe Kaientai monument, near the tip of Meriken Park. Use the front camera, face the water with the statue behind you, and try 0.5x to squeeze more of it in. Check your screen and shuffle until the statue sits nicely over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask your helper to stand in the open area in front of the statue, facing it, so the whole set of figures and the harbour behind fit in the frame, while you pose near the monument.
card.rules_and_safety: This may be an open public space or a place with restricted access, so check for signs or posted restrictions when you arrive.
card.challenge: Take two photos from two distances, one wide shot of the whole scene and one close-up, then see which one you'd actually send to a friend.
card.good_to_know: Kobe Kaientai is spot number 16 on the Kobe map, and it sits near the tip of Meriken Park in front of the sea. We don't have the backstory, so treat this as a record shot of a place you passed. If there's a sign, plaque or name board nearby, photograph that too, so you'll remember what it was later.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 45 m north-east of Kobe Kaientai, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Then walk towards it for a closer shot.

selfie_research.notes: Sources are thin: only Tripadvisor reviews, Mapcarta and a monument database describe this monument, and none of them gives a photo tip or a shooting position. The selfie spot and the photographer position are my inferences from the monument's location near the tip of Meriken Park, its seaside setting, and a review saying the statue stands with the Kobe port behind it. Some review text is in Japanese. Do not confuse this with the nearby BE KOBE monument, which has its own footprint marker and photo guidance; I excluded it because it is a different landmark. No page mentions selfie stick or tripod rules, and no page gives a safety point specific to this monument, so those fields are empty. Verify the exact positions on the ground.
